First-Principles Calculations of the Electron-Hole-Pair Creation Energy in Semiconductors and Dielectrics

Preprint: AIP/123-QED
Dallin O. Nielsen Email: dallin.nielsen@utdallas.edu Affiliation: Department of Materials Science and Engineering, The University of Texas at Dallas, 800 W. Campbell Rd., Richardson, Texas 75080, USA    Massimo V. Fischetti Affiliation: Department of Materials Science and Engineering, The University of Texas at Dallas, 800 W. Campbell Rd., Richardson, Texas 75080, USA
October 12, 2026
Abstract

We present first-principles calculations of the electron-hole-pair creation energy in semiconductors and dielectrics, focusing in particular on AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2. We have employed density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the band structure, density-functional perturbation theory to obtain the phonon dispersion, and time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) to calculate the electron energy loss function (via the dielectric function). We performed full-band Monte Carlo simulations of electron thermalization for energies up to ∼100\sim 100 eV and calculated the average energy required to excite an electron-hole pair. We calculated pair-creation energies of approximately 12.2, 6.5, 7.3, 3.10, and 16.7 eV/pair for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2, respectively. These values are in good agreement with measured data, with the largest discrepancy being that of Si (about 14.9% lower than the accepted experimental value of ∼\sim 3.6 eV/pair). To improve the agreement for Si, we used the GW approach and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) to calculate the quasiparticle shifts of the electronic band structure and the dielectric function, respectively. Finally, using the GW/BSE data, we calculated a creation energy of ∼3.50\sim 3.50 eV/pair. We find that the marked improvement in the accuracy of the calculated creation energy, when using the GW/BSE approach, is primarily attributable to the slight decrease in the magnitude of the electron energy-loss function when using the GW/BSE approach for energies below ∼\sim 10-15 eV. Overall, it is clear that the competition between phonon emission and ionization near the intersection of the phonon scattering and ionization rates is largely responsible for determining the value of the creation energy, with the other major factor being the location and shape of the plasmon peak in the energy-loss function.

I Introduction

When ionizing radiation interacts with a semiconductor or dielectric, it deposits energy mainly by generating electron-hole pairs (EHPs) and, in the case of ions, interacting with the material nuclei. Knowledge of the average energy required to excite or generate an EHP is important for the study of the stopping power and understanding the radiation resistance of a given material and/or device, as well as accurately simulating radiation effects. It is also important in the study of radiation detection [66, 40, 20, 16], photovoltaics [54], radioisotope microbatteries [17, 50], and optoelectronics [6]. This quantity is commonly referred to as the EHP creation energy or radiation-ionization energy [19], typically denoted in the literature by the symbols ϵ\epsilon or WW. In this paper, we will use the symbol ϵ\epsilon to represent the creation energy, following the notation used by McKay [45] and Alig, et al. [3].

In 2023, we published two papers [49, 47], in which we studied, using density functional theory (DFT), the physics of electronic transport in the energy regime of 10-100 eV, an area of study that was previously poorly understood. Following the work of Pines [53] and others [58, 7, 31], we incorporated plasmon emission, impact ionization, and phonon scattering into a full-band Monte Carlo (FBMC) code to simulate carrier thermalization from ∼100\sim 100 eV. Though these papers were primarily focused on developing the physics and understanding the thermalization process, a key result was the calculation of ϵ\epsilon. For GaN, diamond, and β\beta-Ga2O3, we calculated values of 8.9, 12.87, and 11.24 eV [49, 47], respectively. In the present work, we have extended the techniques used in our past works to AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si and SiO2, using not only DFT but also the GW approach and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE), focusing now on the pair creation energy rather than on the dynamics of carrier thermalization. The listed materials have band gaps of 6.2, 2.36, 3.2, 1.12, and 9.0 eV, respectively. This relatively wide range of band gap widths allows for a comprehensive assessment of the predictive power of the first-principles approach in calculating ϵ\epsilon and its dependence on EgE_{g} – a relationship that has been studied since the 1940s, due to its importance in radiation detection and radiation damage.

Bethe developed early analytic approximations of the stopping power of ions in matter that included ϵ\epsilon as a parameter [11], leading to an increased demand for accurate creation energy data to improve radiation damage predictions. Measurements of ϵ\epsilon began in the 1940s and 1950s with the works of Ahearn [1], McKay [45], and McKay and McAfee [44]. Lappe was the first to note that the reported values of ϵ\epsilon were approximately equal to three times the bandgap energy[38], EgE_{\rm g}, a simplification commonly still assumed today. Baldinger and Czaja suggested that the relationship between ϵ\epsilon and EgE_{\rm g} is of the form ϵ=k1​Eg+k2\epsilon=k_{1}E_{\rm g}+k_{2}, a correlation similar to that for gases [8], leading to many attempts to develop such a linear relationship. Some notable examples include those of Shockley [65], Klein [32], and Alig and Bloom [3].

In Fig. 1, the analytic expressions of Klein [32] and Alig et al. [3] are shown along with the measured values of ϵ\epsilon (red circles) for various materials and values that we calculated in past publications [49, 47] (blue triangles), which we mentioned above. It is clear from the figure that both analytic expressions agree well with the measured data for materials with Eg≲3{}_{g}\lesssim 3 eV. For larger bandgaps, the measured creation energies diverge from these analytical predictions as the measured values consistently fall below the two lines. This deviation for wide bandgap materials has led to more recent developments of a new analytic expression [70, 39] with a smaller slope, capturing the data for larger EgE_{\rm g} better at the expense of the fit for small values of EgE_{\rm g}. However, it is clear that the slope of the measured data is not consistent over the entire domain of bandgap energies shown in Fig. 1. Indeed, the divergence seems to increase with increasing bandgap, indicating that, while the qualitative trend is clear, the quantitative relationship between ϵ\epsilon and EgE_{\rm g} is not exactly linear. The agreement between our calculated results and the measured data for GaN and diamond, shown in Fig. 1, suggests that by employing a first-principles approach with a FBMC simulation, one may accurately predict this deviation from the linear behavior.

The present paper is outlined as follows: In Sec. II, we will discuss in more detail the methods used in past works, especially those of Shockley [65] and Alig, Bloom, and Struck[3, 2], along with some lingering questions from their works, which we seek to answer here. We will also discuss why the common linear approximations fail and why a physically more accurate calculation is necessary. In Sec. III, we will show the calculations/simulations for the above-mentioned materials, employing a standard DFT approach, utilizing PBE [52] exchange-correlation functionals. In Sec. IV, to improve the predicted ϵ\epsilon of Si, we will show an alternative calculation of the band structure and the dielectric function, employing the GW approach to calculate the quasi-particle energy shifts in the band structure and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE), which captures the effect of electron-hole interactions, to calculate the dielectric function (the “GW/BSE approach”). Lastly, in Sec. V, we will discuss the results and answer a few questions posed by Alig ert al..

II An Analysis of Past Theoretical Approaches

As mentioned above, a common and longstanding approach to predicting the creation energy has been to develop a linear relationship between ϵ\epsilon and the bandgap energy, EgE_{\rm g}. Early on, in the 1950s, this was done simply by fitting a line to experimentally measured data points without a physical explanation for the fit. Below, we will first discuss in some detail the work done by Shockley in 1961 [65] to attempt to provide such a physical explanation. Afterward, we will discuss the work of Alig, Bloom, and Struck in 1980 [2], who finally moved beyond the assumption of a simple linear relationship. Lastly, we will touch on the more modern MC simulations and why the present work is necessary in the advancement of the state of the art. We will present some questions that remain from the past, which we will attempt to answer in the remaining sections of this paper.

In Shockley’s work, he emphasized the importance of the “competition” between impact ionization and phonon emission during the energy-loss process in determining the value of ϵ\epsilon. When a particle or electromagnetic wave excites an EHP, the excited carriers, if given sufficient energy, will dissipate their energy by causing additional ionization and/or by emitting phonons. After dropping below a certain threshold energy (i.e., below about EgE_{\rm g}), ionization is no longer possible, and phonon emission becomes the dominant energy-loss process. Shockley, therefore, described ϵ\epsilon in terms of the threshold energy, EiE_{i}, the phonon energy, ERE_{R}, the ratio, rr, of the phonon scattering rate to the ionization rate for carriers with E>EiE>E_{i}, and the average carrier energy, EfE_{f}, after falling below EiE_{i}. Following this approach, the general equation for ϵ\epsilon that he obtained is [65]

ϵ=2​Ef+Ei+r​ER.\epsilon=2E_{f}+E_{i}+rE_{R}. (1)

If one employs free-electron bands and assumes that the states below EiE_{i} are ultimately uniformly populated (the “uniform population” assumption [2]), one obtains a value of Ef=0.6​EiE_{f}=0.6E_{i}. The equation for the creation energy then becomes ϵ=2.2​Ei+r​ER\epsilon=2.2E_{i}+rE_{R}. The common approach is to substitute the longitudinal optical (LO) phonon energy for ERE_{R}, assuming that scattering with other vibrational modes is negligible at energies above EiE_{i} [23]. The parameter rr then becomes a fitting parameter, assumed to be constant in energy. Using similar approaches, Klein [32] and Alig and Bloom [3] developed the following equations, ϵ=(14/5)​Eg+0.5\epsilon=(14/5)E_{\rm g}+0.5 and ϵ=2.73​Eg+0.55\epsilon=2.73E_{\rm g}+0.55, respectively (shown in Fig. 1). As measurements of ϵ\epsilon have improved over the years, especially for wide bandgap materials, more recent work [70, 39] has yielded the following equation ϵ=1.54​Eg+1.89\epsilon=1.54E_{\rm g}+1.89. In this newer expression, we see a significant reduction in the slope of the line, due mainly to the divergence shown above in Fig. 1 of ϵ\epsilon from published analytic expressions, as EgE_{\rm g} increases. The issue, as described in the Introduction, is that the relationship between ϵ\epsilon and EgE_{g} is not linear, and attempting to fit a linear curve to the data on one end of the domain of bandgap widths leads to a poor fit on the other end.

While Shockley’s approach cannot account for the measured nonlinear behaviour of ϵ\epsilon as a function of EgE_{\rm g}, it did provide valuable insights. Firstly, it emphasized the importance of the ratio of the phonon emission rate to the ionization rate, which directly led to the work of Alig, Bloom, and Struck (discussed below), whose approach centered on calculating ϵ\epsilon by determining the probability of generating an EHP via the rate ratio. Secondly, it introduced the parameter EfE_{f} to the discussion and raised the question of how the states below EiE_{i} are ultimately populated.

Alig et al. sought to shed some light on the subject by utilizing a new approach which they called the “scattering-rate” assumption [69, 5, 18, 2] with what they called the “probability method”. Instead of assuming that ultimately the states below EiE_{i} are uniformly populated, the scattering rate assumption states that in each scattering event all possible sets of the product particles are created with equal probability. In other words, all nonzero matrix elements for each scattering mechanism (i.e., phonon scattering and impact ionization) are identical and energy-independent. In practice, this means that, when using Fermi’s golden rule to calculate the scattering rates, one may move the matrix elements outside the summation over final states. As an example, Alig approximated the equation for the electron-phonon scattering rates, r(ph)​(E)r^{({\rm ph})}(E) as follows:

r(ph)​(E)\displaystyle r^{({\rm ph})}(E) =2​πℏ​∑j|Mj(ph)|2​δ​(E−Ej±ℏ​ω)\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\sum_{j}\lvert M_{j}^{({\rm ph})}\rvert^{2}\delta(E-E_{j}\pm\hbar\omega)
≈2​πℏ​|M(ph)|2​∑jδ⁡(E−Ej±ℏ​ω).\displaystyle\approx\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\lvert M^{({\rm ph})}\rvert^{2}\sum_{j}\delta(E-E_{j}\pm\hbar\omega). (2)

Here, EE is the energy of the carrier, Mj(ph)M_{j}^{({\rm ph})} is the matrix element for scattering to a state jj of energy EjE_{j}, and ℏ​ω\hbar\omega is the phonon energy absorbed (++) or emitted (−-) in the process. The summation over the delta function simply becomes the total density of states. Alig et al. assumed parabolic, isotropic bands within the free electron model.

The “probability method” involves calculating the probabilities, pn​(E)p_{n}(E), of a primary particle of energy EE generating exactly nn EHPs during the thermalization process. Having calculated pn​(E)p_{n}(E), one may then calculate the average number of generated pairs using the following equation,

⟨n⟩=∑0∞n​pn​(E),\langle n\rangle=\sum_{0}^{\infty}np_{n}(E), (3)

and, finally, the creation energy can be calculated as

ϵ=E/⟨n⟩.\epsilon=E/\langle n\rangle. (4)

We will not include all of the details of the calculation of pn​(E)p_{n}(E) here, but we direct the interested reader to the paper by Alig et al. [2].

A key piece of information needed in the calculation of pn​(E)p_{n}(E) is the ratio of the phonon emission rate to the ionization rate (Shockley’s “r”). By dividing the equation for the phonon scattering rates (Eq. 2) by that for impact ionization via the random-k approximation, Alig et al. obtained the following:

r(ph)​(E)r(ii)​(E)=A​1052​π​(E−ℏ​ω0)1/2(E−Eg)7/2,\frac{r^{({\rm ph})}(E)}{r^{({\rm ii})}(E)}=A\frac{105}{2\pi}\frac{(E-\hbar\omega_{0})^{1/2}}{(E-E_{\rm g})^{7/2}}, (5)

where the parameter A is defined as

A=|M(p​h)|2|M(i​i)|2​32​π4Ωc3​(ℏ22​m)3,A=\frac{\left|M^{(ph)}\right|^{2}}{\left|M^{(ii)}\right|^{2}}\frac{32\pi^{4}}{\Omega_{c}^{3}}\left(\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\right)^{3}, (6)

and Ωc\Omega_{c} is the unit cell volume and ℏ​ω0\hbar\omega_{0} is the longitudinal optical phonon energy. In practice, AA is treated as the single fitting parameter employed in the calculation. Again, we emphasize that according to the “scattering-rate” assumption, the matrix elements are constant, and so, AA is constant.

Alig et al. fit AA to a value of 5.2 so that the method reproduced the experimentally measured value of ϵ\epsilon for Si. Astonishingly, using the same value of AA, they also accurately calculated ϵ\epsilon for several other materials such as Ge, AgBr, and 3C-SiC. For others such as SiO2, C, PbO, and CdS, the method was less accurate. The reasons why Alig’s approach was successful (or not) will be made evident in later sections of this paper. In analyzing their results, Alig et al. raised a couple of important questions that we will attempt to answer in this work: Is the parameter AA constant, or nearly so, for most if not all semiconductors and dielectrics? Is it important to account for plasmon emission, or can it be ignored?

During the 1980s and 1990s, significant advancements were made in simulating electronic transport in semiconductors and solving the semiclassical Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) [28, 63, 67, 22, 21]. These approaches allow one to move beyond the scattering-rate assumption and account for the unequal probability of final-state selection in the scattering process (i.e., unequal and energy-dependent matrix elements). In the following section, we will show the calculations we performed of ϵ\epsilon, using a first-principles approach with MC techniques to solve the BTE.

III Calculating the EHP Creation Energy

III.1 DFT and Scattering Rate Calculations

We utilized the DFT package Quantum ESPRESSO [25] (QE) for all ab initio calculations shown in this section, employing norm-conserving pseudopotentials [60] and PBE [52] exchange-correlation functionals. We began by performing a relaxation of the unit cells of each material, using the vc-relax function in QE. The unit cells of AlN and 4H-SiC are hexagonal, belonging to the P63mc space group, while that of 3C-SiC is zinc-blende with a space group of F-43m, and that of Si is diamond-structured with a space group of Fd3¯\bar{3}m. Finally, for SiO2, we used the α\alpha-quartz structure with space group P3221. The resulting lattice constants, following relaxation, are presented in Table 1.

Using the relaxed structures, we performed self-consistent field calculations to converge the Kohn-Sham potential, using a uniform 8×\times8×\times8 Monkhorst-Pack grid. We then performed non-self-consistent field calculations of the electronic band structures for uniform 40×\times40×\times40 meshes of k points, spanning the first Brillouin Zone (BZ). Using the symmetry operations of each material, these meshes were reduced to irreducible sets of k points spanning the irreducible wedge of each BZ (3234 k points for AlN and 4H-SiC, 1661 for 3C-SiC and Si, and 16422 for SiO2). We calculated and stored the band structure data at these irreducible points for all of the valence bands (VBs) and a sufficient number of conduction bands (CBs) to reach kinetic energies exceeding ∼100\sim 100 eV. The number of necessary CBs varied depending on the material. For Si, we used 136 CBs, while for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, and SiO2, we used 192, 68, 284, 326, respectively. These data were then used for interpolation of the band structure at any arbitrary k and band, nn, in the full-band MC simulations described below.

To incorporate carrier-phonon interactions in our simulations, we employed density functional perturbation theory (DFPT) to calculate the phonon dispersion for the same set of irreducible (q) points as above and all vibrational modes (η\eta) (12 modes for AlN, 6 for 3C-SiC, 24 for 4H-SiC, 6 for Si, and 27 for SiO2). As was done for the band structure, these data were stored in tables for interpolation in the MC simulations.

The carrier-phonon scattering rate between a carrier of wave vector k in band nn and a phonon of wave vector q and branch η\eta was calculated using first-order time-dependent perturbation theory (Fermi’s golden rule) [19],

1τn​(𝐤)≈2​πℏ​∑n′​𝐪|gn​n′η​(𝐤,𝐤′)|2​(N𝐪+1/2∓1/2)×δ⁡[En​(𝐤)−En′​(𝐤′)±ℏ​ω𝐪],\frac{1}{\tau_{n}({\bf k})}\approx\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\sum_{n^{\prime}{\bf q}}|g_{nn^{\prime}}^{\eta}({\bf k},{\bf k^{\prime}})|^{2}\left(N_{\bf q}+1/2\mp 1/2\right)\\ \times\delta\left[E_{n}({\bf k})-E_{n^{\prime}}({\bf k^{\prime}})\pm\hbar\omega_{\bf q}\right], (7)

with

N𝐪=1e(ℏ​ω𝐪/kB​T)−1.N_{\bf q}=\frac{1}{e^{(\hbar\omega_{\bf q}/k_{B}T)}-1}. (8)

Here, gn​n′η​(𝐤,𝐤′)g_{nn^{\prime}}^{\eta}({\bf k},{\bf k^{\prime}}) represents the electron-phonon matrix element, 𝐤′=𝐤±𝐪{\bf k^{\prime}}={\bf k}\pm{\bf q} is the “final” wave vector of the scattered carrier, and n′n^{\prime} is the final band. The upper sign of the plus-minus signs is chosen for absorption, while the lower is chosen for emission. We used Blöchl’s tetrahedron method [12] to evaluate the BZ integration of the delta function. The matrix elements, gn​n′η​(𝐤,𝐤′)g_{nn^{\prime}}^{\eta}({\bf k},{\bf k^{\prime}}), were calculated using the EPW (Electron-Phonon coupling using Wannier functions) code, which is included in the QE package [26, 55]. The matrix elements were calculated on uniform k and q point grids for all VBs of each material and the first 10, 20, 12, 32, and 36 CBs for Si, AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, and SiO2, respectively. As discussed in Ref. [49], the number of necessary CBs is determined by comparing the total phonon scattering rates with the so-called energy-loss rates (which will be discussed below) to find an energy above which phonon scattering becomes negligible.

For electrons and holes possessing kinetic energies greater than the band gap, impact ionization must be considered along with phonon scattering. Additionally, for kinetic energies near and exceeding the bulk plasmon energy, valence-electron plasmon emission must also be taken into account. The plasmon energy of a material can be approximated using the free-electron gas model,

ωp2=e2​nϵ0​m.\omega_{p}^{2}=\frac{e^{2}n}{\epsilon_{0}m}. (9)

Equation (9) yields results of 22.99, 22.99, 22.93, 16.39, and 23.40 eV for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2, respectively. These calculations were carried out using the lattice constants obtained from DFT (see Table 1). As mentioned in the introduction, we calculated the creation energy by simulating the thermalization of electrons with energies up to ∼100\sim 100 eV, and as each of these plasmon energies is well below 100 eV, it was necessary to incorporate plasmon emission as an energy-loss mechanism in the MC simulation. In fact, Pines showed that losses to plasmons are the dominant process in the 10-100 eV energy range [53].

To calculate the total rate of impact ionization and plasmon emission, we utilized the energy-loss function, or the imaginary part of the inverse dielectric function, Im[−1/ϵ(𝐪,ω)]\left[-1/\epsilon({\bf q},\omega)\right], as in Ref. [49]. The loss function is essentially a spectrum that indicates which energies are most likely to be lost when a charged particle interacts with the valence electrons in a material, either via single-particle excitations (impact ionization) or collective excitations (plasmon emission). Using Fermi’s golden rule and the dissipation-fluctuation theorem, we obtained an equation to calculate the total rate of both impact ionization and plasmon emission, which we call the energy-loss rate (ELR),

1τn(ELR)​(𝐤)=2​πℏ​∑n′∫d​𝐪(2​π)3​e2​ℏq2​∫d​ω2​π​Im​[−1ε⁡(𝐪,ω)]×δ⁡[En​(𝐤)−En′​(𝐤+𝐪)±ℏ​ω].\frac{1}{\tau_{n}^{\rm(ELR)}({\bf k})}=\frac{2\pi}{\hbar}\sum_{n^{\prime}}\int\frac{{\rm d}{\bf q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\frac{e^{2}\hbar}{q^{2}}\int\frac{{\rm d}\omega}{2\pi}\ {\rm Im}\left[\frac{-1}{\varepsilon({\bf q},\omega)}\right]\\ \times\delta\left[E_{n}({\bf k})-E_{n^{\prime}}({\bf k}+{\bf q})\pm\hbar\omega\right]. (10)

To calculate the loss function, we utilized the time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) code turboEELS [68], which is included in the QE package. To begin, we performed a standard self-consistent DFT calculation utilizing a 12×12×1212\times 12\times 12 Monkhorst-Pack grid. The output files of this calculation were read by turboEELS, which then calculated the dielectric function for a given wavevector, q. Additionally, we used 1000 Lanczos iterations with a bi-constant extrapolation of the Lanczos coefficients up to 20000 and a Lorentzian broadening of 0.02 eV [49, 47, 48]. As in Ref. [49], we assumed a spherically isotropic loss function in reciprocal space, allowing us to calculate the dielectric function only along a single reciprocal lattice vector for several q points. This approach significantly reduces computational cost, in comparison to a calculation for many q in the irreducible wedge, without appreciably affecting the accuracy of the result [49].

The loss functions of each material are shown in Fig. 2. The primary peaks, which represent the primary bulk plasmons of each material, occur at energies of ∼22.95\sim 22.95, 22.7, 22.7, 17.9, and 25.9 eV for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2, respectively. As the calculations of the plasmon energy using the free-electron gas model showed, the peaks of AlN, 3C-SiC, and 4H-SiC are at nearly equivalent locations. Additionally, the shape and magnitude of the curves for 3C-SiC and 4H-SiC are strikingly similar. One may also observe that the plasmon peak of SiO2 is significantly broader and smaller in magnitude than those of the other materials shown in Fig. 2. This indicates that the uncertainty in the energy of the valence-electron plasmons of SiO2 is higher, and, by Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle, the lifetime (or coherence time) is shorter. The lifetime is controlled by Landau damping, by which a plasmon decays into an electron-hole pair. The relatively flat and broad nature of the SiO2 peak indicates that the plasmons decay more quickly, relative to those in the other materials. Additionally, the broadness of the peak affects the calculated creation energy. While for a narrow peak, electrons with energies above the peak energy will tend to generate pairs with relatively discrete energies, corresponding to the location of the peak, for broad peaks, the pair energy distribution is more continuous. This makes the energy cascade less predictable, requiring more simulations/samples for better statistics.

Looking at Eq. 10, one may also observe that the magnitude of and the area under the loss function curve give a good indication of the trends one may expect to see in the plots of the ELRs. In Fig. 2, up to approximately 28 eV, the magnitude of the loss functions of AlN, 3C-SiC, and 4H-SiC exceed that of SiO2, and it is clear that the areas under the curves, for these three materials, are also larger. One may therefore expect the ELRs of AlN, 3C-SiC, and 4H-SiC to also exceed those of SiO2 over this energy range. The similarities, discussed above, between the loss functions of 3C-SiC and 4H-SiC indicate that the ELRs will likewise be similar.

With the loss functions calculated, we evaluated Eq. 10 for each material. The resulting electron ELRs are shown in Fig. 3.

For each material, the ELRs increase rapidly above the bandgap energy and eventually level off near ∼1017\sim 10^{17} s-1. As one might expect, based on the analysis of Fig. 2, the ELRs of silicon reach this point of leveling off near about 20 eV, just above the plasmon peak energy. These rates level off rather sharply, due to the narrow nature of the loss function peak of Si. For SiO2, the ELRs climb more gradually, which is caused by the much flatter loss function. As is the case for the loss functions, the ELRs of the two polymorphs of SiC are very similar, nearly lying on top of one another over the entire energy range. We also show, in Fig. 4, the total phonon scattering rates (black solid line) with the ELRs for each material (red dashed line). This figure includes the rates for both holes and electrons (separated by the gray shaded region, which indicates the energy gap). As mentioned above, the phonon scattering rates are calculated up to kinetic energies above which the ELRs dominate, rendering phonon scattering negligible.

As discussed in Refs. [49, 47], we note that the relatively large ELRs shown in Fig. 4 may raise questions about the validity of first-order time-dependent perturbation theory (Fermi’s golden rule). This concern has been addressed by Quinn and Ferrell [56, 57], Penn [51], and Pines [53], who found that the electron kinetic energies at which the ELRs are high are large enough to render the broadening of the states acceptably small, justifying the use of first-order perturbation theory.

III.2 Monte Carlo Simulations

With the material properties and scattering rates calculated, we were ready to simulate the thermalization of hot electrons by solving the semi-classical Boltzmann transport equation via full-band MC techniques. Here, we will give only a short overview of the MC simulation, and we direct the interested reader to our previous work [49], which contains the numerical details.

In each material, we initialized a set of electrons (between 1000 and 10000 particles) with kinetic energies chosen under a Gaussian distribution centered at 100 eV (above the CB minimum). Their initial 𝐤{\bf k} points and bands (nn) were chosen by discretizing the BZ and randomly selecting a cell on the BZ mesh, for a given band, that contained the kinetic energy of the electron. A 𝐤{\bf k}-point inside the chosen cell was selected from a set of 𝐤{\bf k}-points on a submesh within the cell, such that the difference between the electron energy and the energy at the 𝐤{\bf k}-point was minimized.

With no applied field, we then simply allowed the electrons to diffuse and scatter via phonon scattering, impact ionization, and plasmon emission. We note that, as in Refs. [49, 47], we assumed immediate decay of emitted plasmons via Landau damping, leading to the creation of an EHP. We justified this assumption in Ref. [49] by showing that the plasmon lifetimes are extremely short, being on the order of ∼10−16\sim 10^{-16} s. This reduces the complexity of the MC simulation, allowing one to treat impact ionization and plasmon emission as effectively identical processes.

As described in Refs. [49, 47], while the electrons possess kinetic energies above ∼10\sim 10 eV, the dominant energy-loss mechanisms are impact ionization and plasmon emission. As shown in Fig. 4, the ELRs are significantly higher than the phonon scattering rates in the energy range of approximately 10-100 eV, about two orders of magnitude higher across much of the range. These relatively high ELRs lead to rapid thermalization, and the electrons lose ∼90%\sim 90\% of their kinetic energy within tenths of a femtosecond. For a visualization of this process, see Fig. 5. After this rapid loss of energy, the thermalization rates slow down markedly, as phonon emission begins to compete with impact ionization. Eventually, the electron energy falls below the threshold for ionization, and the electron energy slowly decays to thermal levels via phonon emission, hindered only by phonon absorption.

As the simulation progressed, we tracked the number of pairs generated in the system by each initially “hot” electron. Using Eq. 4, we then calculated the creation energies of each material. These are shown in Table 2 and plotted in Fig. 6. We note that the magnitude of the creation energy is energy-dependent, as shown by Alig et al. [2], and that the values shown in Table 2 were taken for electron kinetic energies at which ϵ\epsilon saturates. We will discuss this further, below.

We observe remarkably good agreement across the board between the measured data available in the literature and our calculated values. One of the largest discrepancies occurs for SiO2 (a difference of ∼7.6\sim 7.6%). The measurement of ϵ\epsilon for SiO2 was performed in 1975 by Ausman and McClean [7]. By fitting a recombination model to current vs. electric field data obtained by Curtis et al. [15], Ausman and McClean extracted values of ϵ\epsilon for various samples, yielding an average magnitude of ∼18.0\sim 18.0 eV. However, for at least one of the samples, they extracted a magnitude as low as 16.4 eV, which is in much better agreement with our calculated value of 16.7 eV. Additionally, we note that these measurements were performed in 1975 and, as Alig et al. [2] remarked, the general trend is that the measured value of ϵ\epsilon tends to decrease as new measurements are performed using improved instruments with a higher collection efficiency. The fit, therefore, may improve with modern measurements. That said, there does appear to be a tendency for the calculated value to be slightly lower than its measured counterpart. Most notably, this is the case for Si, for which the magnitude of the creation energy is well established. We will discuss why we think this occurs and our attempt to address it in Sec. IV.

Returning to the energy dependence of the creation energy, we have simulated the thermalization of electrons with kinetic energies ranging from 0 to 100 eV in Si, 3C-SiC, and AlN and plotted the results in Fig. 7. From the figure, it is clear that ϵ\epsilon varies significantly for energies below the plasmon peak and then eventually converges to a constant value. As mentioned above, the magnitudes we reported in Table 2 were calculated for kinetic energies of ∼100\sim 100 eV, in the energy range in which ϵ\epsilon is constant. The creation energy becomes approximately energy-independent as the phonon emission rates become negligible relative to the ELRs (ionization plus plasmon emission) and the ELRs level off to a nearly constant value. Because the saturation of ϵ\epsilon occurs at relatively high energies, above the plasmon peak, we conclude that it is important to account for plasmon emission in the simulations. In Sec. V, we will discuss further the importance of plasmon emission in calculating ϵ\epsilon and why Alig et al. obtained reasonable results while ignoring it.

IV The "GW/BSE Approach"

The GW approach has been shown to improve the calculated ab initio bandgap for many materials [64, 14], and the BSE has been used to successfully reproduce the experimentally measured dielectric function of Si [59]. In this section, we will show that in using the GW/BSE approach, we were able to improve the agreement between the predicted and measured values of ϵ\epsilon for Si.

In Sec. III.2, we showed the results of our calculations of the creation energy for various materials, and we observed that the calculated data tended to consistently fall slightly below the measured values. For example, as shown in Table 2, our predicted value of ϵ\epsilon for Si was ∼3.10\sim 3.10 eV, which is about 14.9%14.9\% lower than the well-known measured value of ∼3.6\sim 3.6 eV [61]. Given the success of the GW approach combined with the BSE in reproducing the experimentally measured dielectric function of Si [59], we tested its effect on the calculation of the creation energy.

We utilized the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package [37, 35, 36] (VASP) to perform the GW calculation of the quasi-particle energy shifts and the dielectric function via the BSE. This began with a standard ground-state DFT calculation, including a relaxation of the crystal structure and a self-consistent solution of the Kohn-Sham equations using a 12×12×1212\times 12\times 12 uniform grid of k-points to converge the Kohn-Sham potential. The relaxed lattice parameter from this step was ∼5.47\sim 5.47 Å. With the potential converged, we performed a non-self-consistent calculation of the band structure with 512 unoccupied states (conduction bands).

The primary difference between the standard Kohn-Sham equations and the GW equations is that the exchange-correlation term is replaced by the so-called self-energy Σ\Sigma. In the GW approach, the self-energy is approximated as a Green’s function “G” multiplied by the screened Coulomb potential “W”. Each term depends on the wavefunctions, so one should, in principle, employ a self-consistent technique to solve the equations and converge both “G” and “W”. The primary calculation variants or flavors include G0W0, a single-shot variant in which the quasiparticle energies are calculated in a single iteration; GW0, in which the “W” is held fixed to the initial DFT value while the “G” alone is iterated a user-defined number of times; and GW, in which both terms are iterated. In most cases, GW0 provides the optimal balance of speed and accuracy, and we employ it here.

Finally, we performed a BSE calculation of the dielectric function. The BSE is an equation within the many-body perturbation theory framework used to calculate the excited-state response of materials. Whereas standard DFT calculations employ an independent-particle picture, the BSE accounts for the interaction between the excited electron and hole, known as excitonic effects. As before, we carried out this calculation for several q-points along the first reciprocal lattice vector of Si, again assuming spherical isotropy as in the TDDFT calculations of the loss functions described in Sec. III.1. The computational cost of each calculation for each q-point renders it challenging to obtain the loss function on a fine mesh. However, the loss functions of the materials studied in this work tend to change relatively little for q-points near Γ\Gamma, and due to the 1/q21/q^{2} term in Eq. 10, these points carry the most weight in the calculation of the ELRs and the determination of final states in the MC simulation. Therefore, relatively few points near Γ\Gamma are required to adequately represent the q-dependence of the loss function with little loss in accuracy.

In Fig. 8, we show the loss function of Si calculated using both the TDDFT and GW/BSE approaches for q=0.165q=0.165 Å-1. Firstly, we note that the plasmon peak in the GW result is narrower and has a larger magnitude. It decays more quickly than the TDDFT curve as the electron energy increases above the plasmon peak, while below the peak, the two curves lie nearly on top of one another. To better observe the differences over the energy range below the plasmon peak, we have included an inset figure for electron energies up to 12 eV. It shows that the GW loss function is slightly lower in magnitude for the majority of the range. Although the extent to which it is lower in magnitude is seemingly small, it visibly affects the ELRs near the intersection with the phonon scattering rates, as shown in Fig. 9.

Following the calculation of the loss function and the ELRs, we resimulated the relaxation of electrons in Si and obtained a value of ϵ\epsilon of ∼3.50\sim 3.50 eV. This result is a significant improvement in agreement with the measured value of ∼3.6\sim 3.6 eV. We also calculated the quantum yield and the dependence of ϵ\epsilon on the incident electron kinetic energy. These are shown in Fig. 10 with those calculated by Alig et al. and those measured by Bauer and Ludeke [9]. In all cases, the use of the GW/BSE loss function markedly improved the accuracy of the predicted results. We also note the relatively large effect of seemingly minute changes in the loss function in Fig. 8. From this, it is clear that the rate ratio near the intersection of the ELRs and phonon scattering rates is largely responsible for determining the value of ϵ\epsilon. It can be expected then that further improvements in the prediction will likely come from relatively small changes in the way the phonon scattering rates and ELRs are calculated (i.e., denser k and q Brillouin zone meshes in the calculations of the band structure, phonon dispersion, electron-phonon matrix elements, and dielectric function, variations in the pseudopotentials used, the method employed in handling the exchange-correlation term, etc.).

V Discussion

V.1 Is it accurate to approximate AA as a constant?

Given the success of the methods utilized by Alig et al. [2, 4], for many materials, it is perhaps appropriate to wonder whether there is something fundamental about the assumption that AA is constant. Indeed, a constant value of AA suggests that the ratio of the phonon scattering matrix elements to those of ionization is constant, meaning that the details of the momentum- and energy-dependence of the matrix elements and those of the band structure are negligible for this calculation.

To begin to answer this question, we first rearranged Eq. 5 as follows:

A=r(ph)​(E)r(ii)​(E)​2​π105​(E−Eg)7/2(E−ℏ​ω0)1/2.A=\frac{r^{({\rm ph})}(E)}{r^{({\rm ii})}(E)}\frac{2\pi}{105}\frac{(E-E_{\rm g})^{7/2}}{(E-\hbar\omega_{0})^{1/2}}. (11)

For ℏ​ω0\hbar\omega_{0}, we substituted the longitudinal optical phonon energy (0.063 eV for Si), for r(ph)​(E)r^{({\rm ph})}(E), we used the carrier-phonon scattering rates averaged over equi-energy shells (shown in Fig. 4), and similarly for r(ii)​(E)r^{({\rm ii})}(E), we used the ELRs averaged over equi-energy shells.

In Fig. 11, we show AA as a function of energy for Si and AlN. For Si, we used the ELRs calculated with the GW/BSE approach to calculate AA. Below ∼5\sim 5 eV, for Si, AA is highly variable, while between ∼5\sim 5-13 eV, the magnitude of AA flattens considerably, hovering around ∼4\sim 4. This is relatively close to the value of 5.2 used by Alig et al.. One can therefore say that near the intersection (at ∼5.24\sim 5.24 eV) of the phonon scattering and ionization rates (where the competition between these processes is most important), AA is approximately constant. This fact partly explains why this method works so well for Si. Similarly, for AlN, we observe a flattening of the parameter AA near the intersection of the rates, with a magnitude hovering around a constant value of ∼5\sim 5.

Conversely, in Fig. 12, we also show that for both polymorphs of SiC and for SiO2, AA is not remotely constant over the relevant energy range (near the rate intersection). We can therefore conclude that, while AA may be approximated as constant for some materials, the assumption that it is constant and indeed identical for all semiconductors and dielectrics is unfounded.

V.2 Can plasmon emission be ignored?

One of the conclusions of the paper by Alig et al. is that plasmon emission can be ignored when calculating the creation energy. Given that Alig et al. showed that the creation energy varies with energy and eventually converges to a constant value well above the plasmon energy, this conclusion seems to contradict Pine’s [53] claim that plasmon emission is the dominant energy-loss process in the 10-100 eV range. And the success of the present work (which accounts for plasmon emission) in predicting accurate values of ϵ\epsilon also suggests that plasmon emission is an important part of the calculation. Why then were Alig et al. successful in calculating ϵ\epsilon without plasmon emission, and why, when they included it, did their predictions worsen?

Part of the answer lies in the fact that the parameter AA was specifically fitted to 5.2 so that the method excluding plasmon emission would succeed. Likely, fitting AA separately with plasmon emission included would yield better agreement than simply using the same value of 5.2 (fitted for the case without it). The other part of the answer lies in the ionization rate. Alig et al. calculated the ionization rate using Kane’s random-k approximation. In their approach, however, they employed free-electron bands, while we have employed the full band structure calculated using DFT. The density of states for free electrons is different, and the ionization rates via the random-k approximation are strongly dependent on the density of states, so one may expect significant differences between the ionization rates calculated using free-electron bands and those calculated using full bands.

In Fig. 13, we show the random-k ionization rates calculated using free-electron bands and those calculated using the full band structure of Si. Additionally, we show the ELRs of Si, calculated using the GW/BSE dielectric function. Interestingly, the free-electron ionization rates resemble the ELRs closely but are markedly different from the full-band random-k rates, especially as the kinetic energy increases. This suggests that by employing free-electron bands, one, perhaps by accident, nearly exactly accounts for both impact ionization and plasmon emission without additional effort. Therefore, the work of Alig et al. essentially includes plasmon emission by default, which helps to explain why it is so successful in predicting the energy dependence of the quantum yield and ϵ\epsilon for Si.

V.3 The quantum yield of Si

Lastly, in this section, we briefly discuss the shape of the quantum yield curve of Si, as shown in Fig. 10(b). Specifically, of interest is the “bump” that occurs near ∼4\sim 4 eV, which appears in the calculated results of this work and that of Alig et al. [2] as well as the measured data of Bauer and Ludeke [9]. Above ∼5.5\sim 5.5 eV, the curve becomes approximately linear and no further “bumps” are observed. Here, we will explain the origin of this feature and why the curve becomes smooth as the kinetic energy increases.

The fact that we observe this “bump” in the results of Alig et al. suggests that its origin is not related to the band structure or the (joint) density of states of the material, as Alig et al. employed free-electron bands. Additionally, one may immediately reject the idea that the scattering matrix elements play a role, due to the use of the “scattering-rate” assumption. Instead, one must consider the “probability method” of Alig et al. as a possible origin.

As described above, the “probability method” involves calculating the probabilities pn​(E)p_{n}(E) that a carrier of kinetic energy EE generates exactly nn pairs. In Fig. 14, we show the results of this calculation as published by Alig et al. [2]. Between 4 and 5 eV, p1​(E)p_{1}(E) peaks at a magnitude of ∼0.95\sim 0.95, meaning nearly all carriers with kinetic energies in this range generate exactly 1 pair. In Fig. 10(b), the “bump” in the quantum yield occurs in this same energy range and the magnitude if the quantum yield at this “bump” is ∼1\sim 1. Therefore, the correct interpretation is that the quantum yield flattens at ∼1\sim 1 in the energy range of approximately 4-5 eV, as nearly all carriers excite exactly 1 pair. As the energy decreases, the average number of pairs generated goes below one, as p0​(E)p_{0}(E) increases.

Above ∼5.5\sim 5.5  eV, the quantum yield curve is smooth, resulting from the fact that each successive pn​(E)p_{n}(E) curve is broader and overlaps more with the previous one.

VI Conclusions

Employing a first-principles approach, we have calculated the band structure, phonon dispersion, dielectric function, and electron-phonon matrix elements for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2. Using these material properties, we have evaluated the carrier-phonon scattering rates and the energy-loss rates, which we have incorporated into a full-band MC simulation of the relaxation and transport of electrons and holes. By simulating the thermalization of electrons with kinetic energies as high as 100 eV, we have calculated the creation energies of the listed materials (AlN: 12.2 eV, 3C-SiC: 6.5 eV, 4H-SiC: 7.3 eV, Si: 3.1 eV, and SiO2: 16.7 eV) as well as their energy dependence and that of the quantum yield.

We have shown that this approach yields results that are in good agreement with measured data. We have also shown that improvements in the agreement, in the case of Si, can be made by employing the GW approach to calculate the band structure and the BSE to calculate the dielectric function. Whereas the TDDFT approach yielded a value of ϵ∼3.10\epsilon\sim 3.10 eV, the GW/BSE approach yielded a value of ∼3.5\sim 3.5 eV, which is in much better accord with the experimental value of ∼3.6\sim 3.6 eV. Similar improvements have also been shown in the energy dependence of the quantum yield.

We have also discussed the parameter AA from the work of Alig et al. [2] and shown that while it may be approximated as constant for Si and AlN over a relatively wide energy range near the intersection of the phonon-scattering and ionization rates, this is not the case for 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, or SiO2. Additionally, we showed that plasmon emission must be considered in the calculation of the creation energy, as the creation energy reaches a constant value well above the plasmon peak energy. And finally, we discussed the origin of the “bump” in the quantum yield of Si that occurs near a kinetic energy of ∼4\sim 4 eV, and we found that it is related to the probability of generating exactly one EHP.
